games.summary: Thursday's opener is a protection story. Houston gets home after the pass rush to the tune of a sack on more than 9% of dropbacks, and Indianapolis may be starting backups at both tackle spots on a short week. That's a bad mix for Daniel Jones, who has been the least efficient passer in football over the last three weeks and just watched the front office trade away Josh Downs and Keenan Allen. Stroud has been rolling, and Nico Collins is the best player in either receiver room. The one thing that keeps this from being a walkover on paper is the number: the market has run Houston from about 10 to 12.5, while ESPN's FPI makes it closer to a touchdown. The mismatch is real; whether it's two touchdowns' worth is a different question.

details.scheme: Houston's pass rush (9.2% sack rate, second-best) meets an Indianapolis line that allows 7.1% and may be without both starting tackles (Raimann concussion, Travis doubtful). Jones has been the league's coldest passer over Weeks 8-10 (-0.360/db), and the deadline sell-off (Downs, Allen) left Tyler Warren as the only proven target. Stroud is +0.218/db over the same stretch; Nico Collins (+0.436/tgt) is the best receiver on the field.

games.summary: This is about as lopsided as the efficiency numbers get. Buffalo throws well, converts on third down, and gets a Miami pass defense near the bottom of the league. Miami is down to Kyle McCord, whose first start was rough, behind a line that gives up sacks at one of the highest rates in football. The second-biggest gap on the slate belongs here. The only real caution is the size of the spread: 16.5 already prices in a rout, and Josh Allen's efficiency has dipped over the last three weeks. If Buffalo's two banged-up corners can't go, Miami's receivers get a little more room, but not enough to change who controls this game.

details.scheme: Buffalo's offense is fourth in pass EPA (+0.208) and top-ten on third down (+0.098), and it draws a Miami pass defense allowing +0.161/db (fifth-worst). Miami is on its third quarterback: Kyle McCord was -0.322/db in his first start, and the line allows sacks on 9.2% of dropbacks. Buffalo's one soft spot is a secondary that lost Benford and Alford in-game on Sunday.

games.summary: The matchup to watch is New Orleans' rebuilt offensive line against the best third-down defense in football. The Saints could be down three starters up front, and Chicago gets home often enough to make that a problem every time Shough faces third-and-long. Chicago's own offense isn't as sharp as it was a month ago, and Williams has been around average for three games, but the Bears are still well above New Orleans on third down. The market jumped from about a touchdown to 11.5 after the Saints' line news; FPI is closer to 8. The mismatch is clear. Whether the number has gotten ahead of it depends on who's at center and right tackle on Sunday.

On the other side, Caleb Williams has cooled (-0.025/db Weeks 8-10), but Chicago's third-down offense (+0.149) is top-eight.

games.summary: Neither defense can stop a pass, so this one comes down to which offense is better at taking advantage. That's Dallas, comfortably. Prescott has been efficient all year, Lamb is getting a target share most teams can only dream of, and the Cowboys' line almost never gives up a sack. Tennessee's offense improves when Ward has time, but the Titans are near the bottom of the league at staying on the field on third down, and their best young receiver, Carnell Tate, is still questionable. Dallas also came out of the 49ers shootout with real losses: Ferguson, Bland and Booker are all out. Bland's absence is the one that matters most against Ward. The 54.5 total says points, and the data agrees. The Dallas edge is real but not glaring.

games.summary: On paper this is closer than the spread. Detroit's offense is still better, but Goff has been close to average for three weeks and the Lions' third-down offense has been below average all season. The bigger news is on defense: Aidan Hutchinson tore his ACL in Munich, and Kerby Joseph is still out, so Detroit's season pass-rush numbers overstate what Tampa Bay will face. The quarterback question in Tampa matters less than it seems. Jalon Daniels has actually been more efficient with this offense than Mayfield, whose foot has him in doubt. The Bucs still can't throw well and still give up too many sacks, which keeps Detroit the right side of the mismatch. But at 6.5, with FPI around a field goal, there's more room on the Tampa side than the records suggest.

details.scheme: The smallest gap on the slate. Tampa Bay runs more than it throws (163.9 rush yds/g vs 141.9 passing) into a Detroit run defense that's average (-0.097). The Bucs' pass offense is bottom-three (-0.154), and their line allows 9.2% sacks. But Detroit lost its pass rush engine (Hutchinson, torn ACL) and S Kerby Joseph is still out, so the 8.2% sack rate and pass D numbers (+0.105) behind it are a ceiling, not a floor. Goff is +0.007/db over Weeks 8-10, and Detroit's third-down offense is -0.082 (below average).

games.summary: The best game of the week, and it's a straight test of strength against strength. San Francisco's offense is the best in football, and Purdy has been unreal over the last three weeks. Minnesota's defense brings the league's best pass rush and one of the best third-down units, and the pressure-against-protection fight is where the Vikings can win this. The rest of the numbers lean San Francisco: the Vikings' run game has struggled, the 49ers stop the run, and Minnesota's receiver room is thin without Addison and possibly Hockenson. Cousins is a clear upgrade on what Minnesota had before the trade, though he threw three picks against this defense two weeks ago with the Raiders. Mike Evans' Achilles is the swing factor on the other side. The data favors San Francisco by a bit more than the field goal the market is offering, but not enough to call it a glaring gap.

Minnesota's offense has been below average (-0.100), but Cousins (+0.105/db) is an upgrade on what they had, and SF's run D (-0.116) is strong against a Vikings run game that's -0.167.

games.summary: Monday night features the hottest quarterback in football. Burrow has been nearly untouchable over the last three weeks, and he has two receivers in Chase and Higgins who are both producing at an elite rate. Washington's pass defense has been below average all year and doesn't have the pass rush to speed Burrow up. The reason this isn't a bigger gap is Cincinnati's own defense, which is one of the worst in the league at getting off the field on third down. Daniels and Washington have been poor on third down too, but this is the matchup where they can find some life. The line has moved from about a field goal to 6.5 after Cincinnati's blowout of Pittsburgh, and FPI sits right around seven, so the market has caught up. The edge is real; the number is fair.

details.scheme: Cincinnati's offense is the second-best in football (+0.158 EPA/play) and Burrow is +0.414/db over Weeks 8-10, with Chase (+0.550/tgt) and Higgins (+0.698) both elite.
